extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, in-house counsel and practitioners working on U.S. design patent prosecution and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and prosecution/litigation standards, evidentiary rules, and strategic guidance for asserting, defending, and drafting U.S. design patents (with emphasis on preliminary injunction practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on its preliminary injunction motion, for each asserted patent, Apple must show that it is likely to succeed in establishing that (1) there is infringement, and (2) the patent is not invalid. In addition, Apple must establish that unless the court issues an injunction immediately, Apple will sustain 'irreparable harm,' and that such injunction favors the public's interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden is high in preliminary injunction cases; proving likely success requires both infringement and likely validity; the movant must also show irreparable harm and that injunctive relief serves the public interest. A favorable finding on one issue (e.g., infringement) is insufficient without likely success on validity and the equitable factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use design patents to protect aesthetic aspects (appearance of a cellphone, tablet surfaces, bezels, etc.); use utility patents for functional/internal innovations. This distinction informs claim drafting, asserted rights, and defenses such as functionality-based invalidity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test for design patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove design patent infringement, a patentee must satisfy the 'ordinary observer' test: 'in the eye of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same, if the resemblance is such as to deceive such an observer, inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit (Egyptian Goddess) held the ordinary observer test is the sole test for design patent infringement but it must be conducted 'in view of the relevant prior art.' Consider visual comparisons, market context, and temporal factors that affect the ordinary observer's perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior art when assessing infringement and anticipation (Int'l Seaway effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Egyptian Goddess added that the design patent infringement analysis must be conducted in view of the relevant prior art. International Seaway Trading modified the anticipation test to be the ordinary-observer test in reverse (a lower, more infringement-like standard for anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art can limit scope both for infringement assessment and for validity (anticipation/obviousness). Be aware that Int'l Seaway (panel, not en banc) relaxed the anticipation standard compared to older 'identical in all material respects' precedents (e.g., Hupp). The status of precedent and possible appeals should be considered in strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim and multiple embodiments: 'all or nothing' exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are permitted to have only a single claim; multiple embodiments illustrated must be patentably indistinct, and 'anticipation of any embodiment presented as representative of the concept would defeat the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including multiple embodiments with a single claim increases flexibility to assert infringement (choose an embodiment that best matches accused products) but increases exposure: if any one embodiment is anticipated or obvious, the entire design patent can be invalidated (Ex Parte Appeal No. 315-40; In re Klein). A prosecution strategy is to file separate stand-alone applications for valuable embodiments to avoid 'all or nothing' invalidation, trading off increased filing and issue fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dotted (broken) lines must be accompanied by a specification disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken (dotted) lines depict unclaimed subject matter, but an applicant is required to include a statement in the specification to make it clear if the applicant is disclaiming portions shown in dotted lines. 'Unclaimed subject matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment thereof.' (MPEP 1503.03 III, MPEP §1503.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include the written disclaimer can result in courts construing broken lines as part of the claimed design (see Bernardo Footwear v. Dillard's). If ambiguous, the drawing may be held indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112 (In re Blum). When using dotted lines to disclaim background/environment or features, include explicit specification language clarifying the intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading conveys claim-limiting information about contour and material
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface shading is used to show contour (plane, concave, convex, etc.) and oblique lines are required to depict transparent, translucent, highly polished, or reflective surfaces (MPEP 15.48 and 15.49). Shading in drawings can function as a claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intending to claim a flat glass front face (or a recessed/front contour), use appropriate surface shading (cross-hatching or oblique lines) in the drawings and disclose their meaning in the specification. Lack of shading where contour is relevant can create indefiniteness or allow invalidity challenges; conversely, shading that limits the claim can be used to distinguish prior art that lacks the limited surface characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are effectively the claim — drawing errors can be dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: In the world of design patents, because the drawings are effectively the claim, errors such as inconsistent use of solid vs. dotted lines (e.g., a user's left hand in solid lines) can prove costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully proof drawings and specification statements. Small drafting errors or omissions may create unanticipated claim scope, indefiniteness, or vulnerabilities that litigants will exploit. Examiner amendments and prosecution history may mitigate some errors but the face of the issued drawing controls unless the record clearly disclaims otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history is intrinsic evidence and can clarify drawing ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history is deemed intrinsic evidence; statements made during prosecution (e.g., examiner amendments disclaiming dotted lines) can be used to interpret ambiguous drawings or disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with §112 or claim construction challenges based on drawings, review prosecution records for clarifying statements or examiner amendments. Relying on prosecution history can sometimes rescue an ambiguity on the face of the issued patent, but it's preferable to have clear specification language on the face of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose meaning of dotted lines or shading can render a claim indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112
rubrics_metrics.description: Dotted and broken lines may mean different things in different circumstances and 'in each case it must be made entirely clear what they do mean, else the claim is bad for indefiniteness under 35 USC 112.' (In re Blum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid §112 indefiniteness attacks, explicitly describe the meaning of broken lines and any shading in the specification. Do not rely on the prosecution history as the primary means for clarifying drawing intent whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality challenges must consider overall appearance, not dissected elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a design is primarily functional or ornamental, 'the claimed design is viewed in its entirety... the ultimate question is not the functional or decorative aspect of each separate feature, but the overall appearance of the article.' (L.A. Gear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants' 'divide-and-conquer' functionality arguments or 'masking tape' approaches (ignoring allegedly functional elements) are legally suspect. Focus on overall visual impression; alleged functions of individual features do not automatically render the claimed design invalid if alternative designs exist. Functionality arguments often raise factual disputes for the factfinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: do not 'mask over' functional features without proper legal basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Samsung's counsel attempted to argue functional aspects should be ignored in claim construction (citing Richardson), but such a 'masking tape' approach is flawed and has been rejected in some cases (Good Sportsman Marketing discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing design claims, courts must be cautious about excising features deemed 'functional' absent clear precedent; improper excision could unsettle many design patents. Counsel should prepare to rebut requests to remove features from visual comparison and show existence of alternative designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of multiple embodiments and dotted-line practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple embodiments and liberal dotted line practice can increase the effective scope of a single design patent by allowing a patentee to select an embodiment to match an accused product, but this practice also increases exposure to prior art and to doctrine that a single invalid embodiment can defeat the whole claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination strategy: file multiple-embodiment applications for broad coverage and separate stand-alone applications for particularly valuable embodiments to hedge risks. Consider costs (application, search, issue fees) versus commercial value when choosing prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: European Registered Community Design (RCD) contrasts with U.S. 'all or nothing' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The European RCD system does not follow the 'all or nothing' approach; multiple designs in an RCD application are judged on their own merit and one invalid design does not invalidate others in the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign applicants and practitioners should be aware of systemic differences when formulating global design protection strategies and when deciding whether to pursue separate filings in the U.S. versus grouped registrations abroad. Expect changes as the U.S. implements the Hague Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP practice on broken lines and surface shading
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP guidance: MPEP 1503.03 III 'Broken Lines' (broken lines for environment/unclaimed subject matter must be described); MPEP 15.48 and 15.49 on 'Surface Shading' (use shading to show contour and depict transparent/reflective surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP drawing conventions to avoid rejections and indefiniteness issues. Use explicit specification statements required by MPEP when relying on broken lines; use appropriate surface shading conventions to indicate materials/contours that will limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation/obviousness challenges in design patents: rarity at PTO but significant in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent prior art-based rejections are rare at the PTO (study referenced: only 1.2 percent of design patent applications ever receive a prior art based rejection), but litigation may present close prior art that threatens validity (e.g., Knight-Ridder 1994 prototype, Japanese prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do prior art searches and clearance analyses early; be prepared for aggressive prior art defenses in litigation. Even if PTO practice is lenient on novelty, courts may apply different or evolving standards (e.g., Int'l Seaway) that broaden anticipation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal market context affects scope under the ordinary observer test
rubrics_metrics.description: In initial years of a new product category, differences in later entrants' designs may need to be greater to avoid design patent infringement because 'the ordinary observer' in a nascent category may not yet be able to discriminate between designs—scope may be broadest the day a design patent issues and diminish over time as the ordinary observer develops greater discriminatory faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market maturation when evaluating enforcement prospects and when drafting claims/drawings. Early in a product category, design rights can be especially potent; long-term enforcement may become harder as consumer discernment increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any anticipatory prior art of a represented embodiment can invalidate the entire design claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a single design claim may cover multiple embodiments, 'anticipation of any embodiment presented as representative of the concept would defeat the claim' (T.T.A.B. precedent and In re Klein discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prosecuting multiple embodiments, ensure each embodiment is sufficiently distinct over prior art or consider separate filings. Prepare to defend each representative embodiment against searches and potential invalidating references.
